prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first, but after reading all eight ballots I move to the topological-insulator candidate (B018) as my preferred single-achievement prize. It is the only shortlisted candidate that six of eight members ranked, with two first places and five top-three rankings, and no one who ranked it questioned the science. It has the structure I look for as an experimentalist: a clean prediction (Kane and Mele's Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall state) followed by a decisive measurement (Molenkamp's group seeing edge-channel conductance in HgTe wells), then more than fifteen years of independent confirmation in transport and ARPES across HgTe, InAs/GaSb, Bi-based and three-dimensional materials. The credited trio is a coherent theory-plus-experiment configuration that fits the three-person limit, and the recognition is timely rather than early.
statement.case_against: The attribution is imperfect. The HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what told Molenkamp's group what to build, and the three-dimensional topological insulators (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan) are not represented in this trio. Zhang's death simplifies one allocation but does not remove the objection that the citation leaves out key contributors. There is also a real question whether the 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions already covers the conceptual ground, and the committee must be able to argue that this is a distinct, experimentally established discovery and not a follow-on. Applications remain modest. I am also outside condensed matter and rely on colleagues for relative standing.

responses.point: Ranked topological insulators first for the verified chain from the Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall prediction to the HgTe edge-transport measurement, while flagging that credit for the HgTe proposal and for the 3D case lies partly outside the three names and asking whether the citation should be narrow (quantum spin Hall) or broad (topological insulators).
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-to-measurement chain is what makes this credible, and that persuaded me more than my own IceCube ranking did. On the citation question I side with the narrower reading: the prize should rest on the Z2 time-reversal-invariant class and the quantum spin Hall state with its HgTe realisation, and I would not try to stretch it to the 3D materials, where Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan would raise exactly the allocation problem you describe. I would like you to say plainly whether you think a narrow citation is defensible without the BHZ proposal, since you know the field far better than I do. If it is not, B018 is weaker than the vote count suggests.

responses.point: Ranked topological insulators third, noting that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio but that the 2016 topological-phases prize may be argued to already cover the field. He also ranked IceCube second and flagged that a single-name credit for a large collaboration is a simplification.
responses.response: The 2016 overlap is the strongest objection to B018, and I take it seriously. My answer is that the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type topological phases in one and two dimensions, whereas time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are a separate class that was predicted and then observed. I accept your reservation about IceCube and it moved me off my opening position: a sole credit to Halzen for a roughly 300-author collaboration, with AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors, is hard to defend as written. I would ask you whether a revised IceCube credit with more than one name exists that the committee could support; if it does, I would revisit it.

responses.point: Ranked optical lattice clocks first for 1e-18 uncertainties and new measurements in fundamental constants and geodesy, regarded Katori plus Ye as a clean two-person configuration, and wondered whether it sits too close to the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
responses.response: I rated clocks sixth in my opening ballot and I think I under-weighted them. The independent confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE is exactly the kind of systematics-driven validation I respect, and I find your argument that this is a new measurement regime rather than an engineering refinement convincing. My reservation is timing and ordering. The SI second redefinition is still pending, and Ye already holds a 2005 prize share for the comb. I do not think either is disqualifying. I keep B041 as my first alternative and would prefer it to a second pass at AMO quantum-simulation candidates, where the five-name problem remains.

responses.point: Ranked circuit QED first as the architecture of superconducting quantum processors and the natural successor to the 2025 prize, while openly flagging professional proximity to the community and the Girvin-versus-Blais choice under a three-person cap.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged your proximity yourself. My concern is not that circuit QED is unimportant but that the committee just gave the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and returning to the same community immediately risks looking repetitive. The four credited names also cannot fit under the three-person cap without leaving out a decisive contributor, which also affects B020. Only two members ranked it, and I have not seen an argument that it needs to be settled this year. I would like to hear whether you think waiting a few years costs anything.

responses.point: Ranked fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics first, ranked topological insulators second, and framed the prize as completing a coherent picture in statistical and condensed-matter physics.
responses.response: Your second-place support for B018 is useful because it comes from a theorist who would be hard on an overstated prediction. On B032 my difficulty is attribution and verification, not importance. Jarzynski, Crooks, Evans and Seifert contributed different pieces, and I cannot see how a three-person split is made without arbitrary choices. The experimental confirmation is mainly in small colloidal and biomolecular systems rather than in an independently reproduced headline measurement. Please correct me if the attribution is cleaner than I think.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend a citation that excludes Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe proposal and the three-dimensional topological insulator discoveries.
Whether the 2016 prize for topological phases is judged to leave room for a separate time-reversal-invariant topological insulator prize.
Whether IceCube can be credited to a defensible group of up to three people, since a sole credit to Halzen seems unlikely to survive scrutiny.

Whether the committee prefers a single topological prize or a two-part prize with a precision-measurement achievement such as optical lattice clocks, which the three-person limit makes hard to configure fairly.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018, B041 or B016. My work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur, balloon polarimetry) is in astroparticle physics, so I know the IceCube neutrino and Daya Bay reactor communities only as neighbouring fields, and I have no listed collaboration with any credited candidate.
